doc: The first mission, guided (C9, issue #14): what the crew coach says on each screen and design step, and what it lights up. ctx is a screen id, or design:<step index>; who is the station whose bot speaks; targets are the visible texts of the options or buttons to light. The design they lead to (medium platform; multispectral camera, gamma-ray spectrometer, radar altimeter; large solar wings and the 1 kWh battery; Ka band; wheels and star tracker; chemical propulsion; medium launcher) was checked with Mission.compute(): no warning, 243 M$ of 380.

tips.title: Welcome aboard
tips.text: Your first mission: land at the Moon's south pole, where the Sun never climbs high and ice may hide in the dark of the craters. First, the extra goals: keep the ones you want to go for and press Continue. Then the orbit, where your craft will fly: lunar orbit, 100 km up, is the one. Click it.

tips.title: The body of the craft
tips.text: The platform is the craft's body: structure, computer, room for instruments. A small one is cheap but fills up fast. Take the medium platform: room for three instruments, and strong enough to carry fuel to the Moon.

tips.title: What we came to see
tips.text: The goal needs two things: look for ice in the shadows, and photograph the landing site. A gamma-ray spectrometer reads what the ground is made of; a multispectral camera sees the site in many colours; a radar altimeter measures the ground's height. Every instrument costs mass, power and data: watch the board on the right.

tips.title: Power
tips.text: Instruments need watts. Large solar wings make enough, and the 1 kWh battery covers the hours in shadow. If the wings glow amber on the craft, power falls short: that is the craft telling you.

tips.title: Bringing the data home
tips.text: Every photo has to come home. Ka band is the fastest antenna: it sends all of today's data, today. A slower radio loses science, and its antenna would glow amber.

tips.title: Pointing and pushing
tips.text: Sharp photos need precise pointing: reaction wheels and a star tracker. To brake into lunar orbit and land you need delta-v, a change of speed. Chemical propulsion gives 1,500 m/s.

tips.title: The ride up
tips.text: The farther the destination, the less a rocket can carry. The medium launcher lifts your craft toward the Moon: click it. Feeling brave? Build your own rocket instead, from the engines up.

tips.title: Your own rocket
tips.text: We build it from the ground up, one choice at a time: engines, tank, an upper stage, the fairing. In a hurry? Take the ready Falcon 9-type. When the three answers on the right are ticked, fly it.

tips.title: The review
tips.text: Real NASA teams check a design like this before it flies. Blue is fine, amber costs science, red stops the launch. Nothing red? Then it is yours to fly. Press LAUNCH!

tips.title: You fly it
tips.text: Keep the needle on the green marker with the arrow keys. When a stage runs dry, press Space to drop it: the rocket gets lighter and goes faster. Time runs for real; speed it up with the time controls.

tips.title: Toward the Moon
tips.text: In orbit around the Earth. Mission control planned the departure: about 3,200 m/s burned at the right moment, then about three days of coasting, as Apollo 11 did. Look at the path, then give the GO: the flight computer fires the engine at the planned second.

tips.title: Touchdown
tips.text: Shackleton's rim, near the south pole. More throttle slows the fall; touch down slower than 3 m/s. If alarm 1202 rings, keep calm: Apollo 11's computer raised it too, and they landed.

tips.title: Now it works
tips.text: You made it. Now the mission does its job: months go by, data comes home, surprises happen. A good design rides them out.

tips.title: What you found
tips.text: Your report: the science, the real NASA photos a mission like yours sends home, and the real missions like it. There is no perfect design. Try another, and beat your score.
